etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old English hēræfter (“in the aftertime; later on”). By surface analysis, here +‎ after.

definitions.definition: (dated) In time to come; in some future time or state.

quote.citation: c. 1606, William Shakespeare, “Act V Scene V”, in Macbeth:
quote.text: She should have died hereafter; / There would have been a time for such a word.

quote.citation: 1693, John Dryden, The Last Parting of Hector and Andromache, translation of The Iliad by Homer:
quote.text: […]  when hereafter he from war shall come /  And bring his Trojans peace and triumph  […]

definitions.definition: Sequentially after this point (in time, in the writing constituting a document, in the movement along a path, etc.)

quote.citation: 1712, Joseph Addison, Cato, a Tragedy, act 5, scene 1:
quote.text: 'Tis the Divinity that stirs within us; / 'Tis Heaven itself that points out an hereafter, / and intimates eternity to man.
